tool.name: n8n
tool.tagline: Fair-code workflow automation with a visual editor, AI agents and self-hosting
tool.description: n8n is a workflow automation tool: you connect nodes on a canvas so that an event (a form entry, a webhook, a schedule) flows through steps that read, transform and send data between apps. It has hundreds of integrations, an HTTP Request node for any API, a Code node for custom logic, and LangChain-based AI nodes for building agents. You can use n8n Cloud or run it yourself with Docker, which makes it popular with teams that want control over their data.

glossary.def: In n8n, one automation: a chain of connected nodes, started by a trigger, that passes data from step to step.
One box on the n8n canvas that does one job, such as sending an email or checking a condition. Nodes are connected into workflows.
The first node of an n8n workflow: the event that starts it, such as a schedule, a form entry or a new email.
One run of an n8n workflow, saved with the data every node received and produced.
In n8n, one setting of a node, such as which spreadsheet to use or who to email; shown in the middle panel when you open the node.
One record of data passed between n8n nodes, like one row of a spreadsheet: one customer, one email, one order. Most nodes run once per item.
In n8n, a small formula inside {{ }} in a node setting that n8n replaces with a real value, such as the current item's email, when the node runs.
n8n's licence model: the program's code is public and you may run it yourself, but reselling it as a service is restricted.
The version of n8n that the n8n company runs for you; you just sign up and use it in your browser.
Running a piece of software on computers you control yourself, instead of using the maker's online service.
The common way to let one service use your account on another without giving it your password: you sign in on the other service's own page and approve the access.
Customer relationship management app: software where a business keeps its contacts, customers and sales deals, such as HubSpot or Salesforce.
An n8n node that adds, renames, changes or removes fields on each item (called Set in older versions).
An n8n node that turns a list inside one item into separate items, one per entry.
n8n's record of which output item came from which input item, so an expression can find the matching data in an earlier node.
The n8n node that sends a web request to any service with an API, for services that have no ready-made node.
An n8n node that sends items through a set of steps in groups of a chosen size, one group at a time (formerly Split in Batches).
In n8n's Loop Over Items node, how many items go through the loop together in each round.
A Webhook node's live address, which works once the workflow is published. The separate test URL only works while you are listening for a test event in the editor.
A popular free toolkit for building apps on large language models; n8n's AI nodes are built on it.
n8n's AI building block: one main root node with smaller sub-nodes (a model, memory, tools) plugged in underneath.
The main node of an n8n cluster, such as the AI Agent, into which sub-nodes are plugged.
A small n8n node plugged into a root node to give it a part it needs, such as the chat model, memory or a tool.
An n8n sub-node that stores the earlier messages of a conversation so an AI agent can refer back to them.
An n8n sub-node that makes a model's answer come back in a fixed shape, such as named fields, instead of free text.
An n8n AI node that sorts each piece of text into one of the categories you define.
An n8n node setting that tries a failed node again a few times, with a pause in between.
An extra exit on an n8n node: items that fail go down it, so you can handle them while good items carry on.
An n8n node that deliberately fails the run with your own message, for example when required data is missing.
The n8n trigger node that starts an error workflow when another workflow's live run fails.
A separate n8n workflow, started by the Error Trigger, that is run whenever a chosen workflow fails, usually to send an alert.
An n8n workflow that is started by another workflow, receives data from it and hands results back, so shared steps are built once.
The trigger node that starts a sub-workflow when another workflow calls it (shown as "When Executed by Another Workflow").
The n8n node that runs a short program you write in JavaScript or Python.
A separate helper program that runs the Code node's code apart from n8n itself, so faulty code can't harm n8n.
An n8n agent tool that uses the tools offered by an outside MCP server.
An n8n trigger node that turns one workflow into its own MCP server, offering the tools attached to it to AI assistants.
An n8n sub-node that cuts long documents into small passages (chunks) before they are stored for search.
A popular tool that runs software inside containers: sealed boxes holding a program and everything it needs, so it runs the same on any computer.
A Docker tool that describes several containers (for example n8n and its database) in one settings file and starts them together.
A Docker storage folder that lives outside a container, so the data in it survives when the container is restarted or replaced.
The secret n8n uses to scramble and unscramble saved credentials. Lose it and the saved credentials can no longer be read.
A popular, free and sturdy database, recommended for running n8n in production.
A small database stored in a single file, n8n's default for simple setups.
A very fast database that keeps its data in a computer's working memory, often used as a waiting line or short-term store.
An n8n setup for heavy load: a main instance puts executions in a waiting line, and separate workers take them and run them.
In n8n queue mode, the copy of n8n that serves the editor, receives triggers and queues executions for workers.
An extra n8n copy in queue mode whose only job is receiving incoming webhook calls, for very high traffic.
The most widely used system for recording every change to a set of files, so versions can be compared, shared and restored.
What n8n sends to Git in place of a credential or variable: only its name, type and ID, never the secret value.
Server-side request forgery: tricking a server into sending requests to addresses it shouldn't, such as a company's internal systems.
Logging in with two proofs instead of one, usually your password plus a code from your phone.

concepts.name: What n8n is: workflows, cloud or self-hosted
concepts.summary: Understand what n8n does, how a workflow is built from nodes, and the difference between n8n Cloud and self-hosting.
concepts.why: Knowing what n8n is good at, and how it is offered, helps you decide how to start.
concepts.body:
Imagine every new website signup should be added to your mailing list, checked against your customer database, and announced in your team chat. n8n (say "n-eight-n") lets you build that as a **workflow**: a chain of steps that runs automatically.

Each step is a **node**, a box on a canvas that does one job: "Gmail: send email", "Google Sheets: add a row (one new line) to a spreadsheet", "If: check a condition". You draw lines between nodes, and data flows along the lines from left to right.

The first node is a **trigger node**: the event that starts the workflow, such as a schedule or a new form entry. Every node after it reacts to the data it receives.

What makes n8n different from tools like Zapier:

- It shows the actual data at every step, so you can see exactly what each node received and produced.
- It has strong building blocks for decisions (checking conditions, repeating steps, combining data) and lets you add small pieces of code when needed.
- It is **fair-code**. Its **source code** (the written instructions that make up the program) is public, and you may run it yourself, under a licence that limits reselling it as a service.

You can use it in two main ways:

- **n8n Cloud**: n8n runs it for you on its own computers, and you use it through its website. "The **cloud**" just means computers you use over the internet instead of your own. Easiest start.
- **Self-hosted**: you run n8n on your own **server** (a computer that stays switched on to run programs for others) or your own laptop, usually with a tool called Docker, covered later. The free community edition has almost all features; paid licences add team and enterprise features.

This course uses n8n 2.x. Many older tutorials show 1.x screens, which differ in places such as how workflows go live.
takeaways: A workflow is a chain of nodes started by a trigger
n8n shows the real data at each step and handles complicated decisions well
Use n8n Cloud, or self-host the fair-code version yourself

quiz.q: What is a node in n8n?
options: One step in a workflow that does one job
quiz.explain: Workflows are built by connecting nodes, each doing one task such as sending an email.

concepts.name: The editor: canvas, nodes and test runs
concepts.summary: Find your way around the editor: add and connect nodes, open a node's input and output, and run the workflow manually.
concepts.why: Everything in n8n is built and fixed in the editor, so moving around it confidently saves hours.
concepts.body:
Open a new workflow and you see an empty **canvas**. Click the plus button (or press Tab) to search for nodes. Nodes come in a few kinds:

- **Trigger nodes** start a workflow.
- **App nodes** work with one service, such as Slack, Notion or Airtable. Each offers actions like "create", "get" or "update".
- **Core nodes** are general tools, such as If (check a condition), Merge (combine data) and Wait (pause for a while).

Drag from one node's small output dot to the next node's input to connect them. Data travels along these connections.

Double-click a node to open it. You see three panels:

- **INPUT** on the left: the data that arrived from the previous node.
- **Parameters** in the middle: the node's settings, such as which spreadsheet to use.
- **OUTPUT** on the right: what the node produced the last time it ran.

You can view data as a table, as JSON, or as a list of just the **field** names. A field is one named piece of data, such as `email` or `price`.

To try things, click **Execute workflow** at the bottom of the canvas, or run a single node with its own execute button. Each run is called an **execution**. During building, executions use your test data and show their results right on the canvas: green ticks for success, red for errors.

Useful habits: rename nodes to say what they do ("Get customer by email" rather than `HTTP Request1`), add sticky notes to explain sections, and run often while building rather than all at the end.
takeaways: Trigger nodes start workflows; app and core nodes do the work
Each node shows INPUT, parameters and OUTPUT
Run the workflow or single nodes often while building
pitfalls: Leaving default node names, which makes later steps that refer to nodes by name, and hunting down problems, confusing.

quiz.q: Where do you look to see exactly what data a node received?
options: The OUTPUT panel of that node
The INPUT panel of that node
quiz.explain: The INPUT panel shows the data that arrived from the previous node.

concepts.name: Trigger nodes: how workflows start
concepts.summary: Choose the right trigger: manual, schedule, app events, forms, chat or web addresses other systems call.
concepts.why: The trigger decides when your workflow runs and what data it starts with.
concepts.body:
Every workflow that runs on its own starts with a **trigger node**. Common ones:

- **Manual Trigger** ("When clicking Execute workflow"): only runs when you click. Good for building and one-off jobs.
- **Schedule Trigger**: runs on a timetable, such as every day at 8:00 or every 15 minutes. Check the **time zone** (which region's clock it follows) in the workflow settings.
- **App triggers**: many app nodes have a trigger version, such as "Gmail Trigger: on message received" or "Google Sheets Trigger: row added". Some are notified instantly by the app; others check for changes on a timer (called **polling**).
- **n8n Form Trigger**: n8n creates a simple online form for you, and each submission starts the workflow.
- **Chat Trigger**: a chat window for talking to an AI assistant you build in n8n (covered in the AI chapter).
- **Webhook**: a web address that any other system can send data to, to start the workflow (its own lesson later).
- **Error Trigger** and **Execute Workflow Trigger**: special triggers for reacting to failures and for workflows started by other workflows, covered later.

A workflow can have more than one trigger, for example a schedule plus a manual trigger for testing.

In n8n 2.x the old "Start" node no longer exists; use the Manual Trigger instead.

Important: most triggers only fire on their own after the workflow is **published** (made live, covered in a later lesson). While building, you start them by hand or use a "listen for test event" button.
takeaways: Manual, Schedule, app, Form, Chat and Webhook triggers cover most needs
App triggers are either instant or polling
Triggers fire automatically only after the workflow is published

quiz.q: You want a report built every Monday at 9:00. Which trigger fits?
quiz.explain: The Schedule Trigger starts workflows on a timetable.

concepts.name: Credentials: connecting your accounts
concepts.summary: Create credentials so nodes can log in to your apps, and understand how n8n keeps them safe.
concepts.why: App nodes can't do anything until they have permission to use your accounts.
concepts.body:
Before a Gmail node can send email from your account, n8n needs permission. That permission is stored as a **credential**: saved login details for one service.

You can create a credential from the node itself (the "Credential to connect with" dropdown) or from the Credentials list. Depending on the service, you either:

- **Sign in with OAuth** (the usual "Sign in with Google" style of login): a window from the service asks you to allow n8n access. n8n never sees your password; it receives a permission pass instead.
- **Paste an API key**: a long secret code from the service's settings page. Treat it like a password.
- Enter a username and password, or other details such as a database address.

n8n tests a credential when you save it and tells you if it works. Rename it to say what it is for, such as "Gmail - support inbox".

How n8n protects credentials:

- They are stored **encrypted** (scrambled so they're unreadable without a secret key). Self-hosters must keep that key safe, as the hosting lessons explain.
- When you share or export a workflow, the credentials themselves are not included, only a note of which credential each node uses.
- Many credentials have a setting (`Allowed HTTP Request Domains`) that limits which websites they may be sent to.

On n8n Cloud, some AI nodes can run without your own credential by using n8n's built-in credits.

In teams, credentials live in **projects** or your personal space, and can be shared with colleagues without revealing the secret values.
takeaways: A credential is n8n's saved, encrypted permission to use an account
OAuth = sign in through the service; API key = secret code you paste
Workflows point to credentials; exports don't contain the secrets
pitfalls: Pasting an API key directly into a node field or into custom code instead of storing it as a credential.

quiz.q: You export a workflow to share with a colleague. What happens to the credentials it uses?
options: Only a note of which credential to use; the secrets stay in your n8n
They are included in plain text
They are emailed to the colleague
quiz.explain: Workflow files point to credentials by name and ID but don't contain the secret values.

concepts.name: Data between nodes: items and JSON
concepts.summary: Learn how n8n passes data: nodes pass a list of items, each item holds JSON fields, and most nodes run once per item.
concepts.why: Almost every confusing result in n8n comes from not knowing how many items flowed into a node.
concepts.body:
Data in n8n is passed between nodes as a list of **items**. Think of an item as one row in a spreadsheet: one customer, one email, one order.

Each item stores its fields as **JSON**, a common text format for data. JSON writes data as `"name": value` pairs inside curly braces. Values can be text in quotes, numbers, true/false, a list in square brackets, or another set of curly braces (a **nested** group of fields, like an address inside a customer). The example shows two items.

Under the hood n8n keeps each item's fields inside a part labelled `json`, and items carrying files (a PDF, an image) also have a part labelled `binary`. You rarely need to type this yourself; the editor shows it.

The key rule: **most nodes run once for each incoming item.** If a Google Sheets node outputs 50 rows, a following Gmail node sends 50 emails, one per row, each using that row's data. You don't need to tell it to repeat.

This rule explains many surprises:

- "Why did it send 50 messages?" Because 50 items arrived.
- "Why did nothing happen?" Because 0 items arrived (the previous node found nothing).

The item count appears on each connection line and in each panel, so check it whenever a result looks wrong.

If you really want a node to act once regardless of how many items arrive, turn on **Execute Once** in the node's Settings tab; it then uses only the first item.
takeaways: Nodes pass a list of items; each item holds JSON fields
Most nodes run once per incoming item
Check the item count when results look wrong
pitfalls: Expecting one Slack message but sending one per item because many items reached the node.

quiz.q: A node outputs 12 items into a "Send email" node. By default, how many emails are sent?
quiz.explain: Most nodes run once per incoming item, so 12 items produce 12 emails.

concepts.name: Mapping fields with expressions
concepts.summary: Drag fields from the input into parameters, and read the {{ $json.field }} expressions this creates.
concepts.why: Expressions are how each node uses the data of the current item instead of fixed values.
concepts.body:
When you configure a node you usually want values from earlier data: send the email to this item's address, not to a fixed one. n8n does this with **expressions**: small formulas inside double curly braces, `{{ ... }}`, that n8n replaces with a real value when the node runs.

The easy way: open a node, find the field in the INPUT panel and **drag** it into a parameter. n8n writes the expression for you, for example `{{ $json.email }}`. Read it as "the `email` field of the current item". `$json` always means the current item's data.

Every parameter has a **Fixed / Expression** switch. Fixed means the text is used exactly as typed. Expression means anything inside `{{ }}` is calculated. Below an expression field, n8n shows a live preview of the result for the current item, which is the fastest way to check you got it right.

You can mix text and expressions:

- `Hello {{ $json.name }}, your order {{ $json.orderId }} has shipped.`
- Nested data uses dots: `{{ $json.address.city }}`.
- Small changes work inline: `{{ $json.name.toUpperCase() }}` turns the name into capital letters.

Because most nodes run once per item, the same expression gives each item its own value.

Expressions are written in the style of JavaScript, a **programming language** (a precise written language for instructing computers) best known for making websites interactive, but you only need the simple forms above to start. The next lessons add data nodes and more expression tools.
takeaways: Expressions in {{ }} are calculated for each item
$json means the current item's data; dots reach nested fields
Switch parameters between Fixed and Expression, and check the preview
pitfalls: Typing {{ $json.email }} into a field left in Fixed mode, which sends those exact characters instead of the email address.

quiz.q: What does {{ $json.address.city }} return?
options: The city of the first item only
The city field inside the address of the current item
quiz.explain: $json is the current item, and dots step into nested fields.

concepts.name: Saving, publishing and executions
concepts.summary: Understand n8n 2.x autosave and Publish, why live runs use the published version, and how to read past executions.
concepts.why: A workflow only runs on its own once published, and the Executions list is where you check what really happened.
concepts.body:
In n8n 2.x your edits **save automatically** within a few seconds, and each change is kept in the workflow's version history. Saving is not the same as going live.

To make a workflow run on its own, click **Publish** (top right). Publishing makes the current version live: schedules start, app triggers listen, and webhook and form triggers use their **production** addresses. Production means the live version that runs for real, as opposed to your test runs. You can name the published version and add a description.

Afterwards you can keep editing. Your changes stay as a draft, and production keeps running the last published version until you publish again. This replaces the Active/Inactive switch of n8n 1.x, so older tutorials that say "activate the workflow" mean "publish".

**Unpublish** takes the workflow out of production. Version history lets you restore an older version or publish a different one, which is how you undo a bad change (a **rollback**).

Every run is an **execution**. The workflow's **Executions** tab lists them with status (success, error, running, waiting) and time. Open one to see the data at every node, exactly as it was. Production runs are only visible here, not on the editing canvas.

Two settings worth knowing:

- Which executions to save (all, or only failed ones), which matters for privacy and for how much storage busy workflows use.
- The workflow's time zone, used by Schedule triggers.

Only one person can edit a workflow at a time; others see it read-only.
takeaways: Edits autosave; Publish makes a version live
Production runs the last published version until you publish again
The Executions tab shows the data of every past run
pitfalls: Editing a live workflow and forgetting to publish, then wondering why production still behaves the old way.

quiz.q: You fixed a mistake in a published workflow and the editor shows your change. Production still has the mistake. Why?
options: The fix is in the draft; you must publish again
Executions are cached for a day
quiz.explain: Production runs the last published version; draft edits go live only when you publish.

concepts.name: Edit Fields and other data nodes
concepts.summary: Reshape data without code using Edit Fields (Set), Filter, Sort, Limit, Remove Duplicates, Split Out and Aggregate.
concepts.why: Cleaning and reshaping data is most of the work in real workflows, and these nodes do it visibly.
concepts.body:
Data rarely arrives in the shape the next app wants. n8n has small **data nodes** for common reshaping jobs, so you don't need code.

- **Edit Fields (Set)**: add, rename or change fields, and optionally keep only the fields you list. Example: create `fullName` from `{{ $json.first }} {{ $json.last }}`, and drop everything else.
- **Filter**: keep only items that meet conditions, such as `amount` greater than 100. Items that fail are dropped.
- **Sort** and **Limit**: order items and keep the first N, such as the top 10 by score.
- **Remove Duplicates**: drop repeated items, compared by all or chosen fields.
- **Split Out**: turn a list inside one item into separate items. One order with 3 products becomes 3 items, so the next node runs 3 times.
- **Aggregate**: the opposite, gathering a field from many items into one list inside a single item (combining many into one is called **aggregation**), useful before sending one summary message.
- **Summarize**: count, sum or average, grouped by a field, like a summary table in a spreadsheet.
- **Date & Time**: format dates and add or subtract time.

When should you use an expression and when a node? Expressions are fine for small changes inside one field. Data nodes are clearer for anything that changes the number of items or the structure, and they show their result in the OUTPUT panel, which makes mistakes easy to find.

Split Out and Aggregate are especially important: they let you switch between "one item with a list" and "many items", which controls how many times later nodes run.
takeaways: Edit Fields adds, renames and drops fields
Filter, Sort, Limit and Remove Duplicates clean up item lists
Split Out makes many items from a list; Aggregate makes one item from many

quiz.q: You have 40 items and want to post ONE Slack message listing all names. Which node helps most before the Slack node?
quiz.explain: Aggregate gathers the names from 40 items into one item, so Slack runs once.

concepts.name: IF and Switch: branching
concepts.summary: Send items down different branches with the If node (true/false) and the Switch node (many routes).
concepts.why: Real business rules treat cases differently: urgent vs normal, paid vs free, found vs not found.
concepts.body:
**Branching** means sending different items down different paths. n8n has two main nodes for it.

The **If** node checks conditions and has two outputs: **true** and **false**. Each condition compares a value (often an expression like `{{ $json.amount }}`) with something. You pick the comparison from a menu sorted by kind of value: text, number, date, true/false, list, or "exists / is empty". Combine several conditions with AND or OR.

Because n8n works item by item, one If node can split a group of items: of 20 orders, 5 go out of "true" and 15 out of "false", and each branch continues with only its own items.

The **Switch** node is for more than two routes. In **Rules** mode you add a rule per output (output 0: country is "US"; output 1: country is "DE"...). Turn on a **fallback output** to catch items no rule matched, so nothing silently disappears. In **Expression** mode, an expression returns the output number directly.

Tips:

- Choose the right kind of value (its **data type**). Comparing numbers as text gives wrong results (as text, "100" comes before "20").
- Check both outputs while testing; an empty branch simply doesn't run.
- The Filter node is the simpler choice when you just want to drop items rather than route them.

After branching you often want to bring the data back together, which is the Merge node's job.
takeaways: If routes each item to true or false
Switch handles many routes; add a fallback output
Use the correct data type (text, number, date...) in conditions

quiz.q: 20 items enter an If node; 6 match the condition. What happens?
options: Only the first item is checked
6 go out of true and 14 out of false
quiz.explain: The If node evaluates each item and routes it to the matching output.

concepts.name: Merge: combining branches and data
concepts.summary: Bring branches back together and join data from two sources with the Merge node's Append, Combine and Choose Branch modes.
concepts.why: Many workflows fetch data from two places and must join them, like a lookup across two spreadsheets.
concepts.body:
The **Merge** node waits for data on two or more inputs and combines it. Its modes:

- **Append**: output all items from input 1, then all from input 2 (and more inputs if added). Use it to rejoin branches after an If node.
- **Combine** with **Matching Fields**: pair items whose field values match, like matching customers from your **CRM** (the app where a business keeps its customer contacts) with invoices from billing by `email`. You choose whether to keep only matches, non-matches, or everything. This is the n8n version of a spreadsheet lookup (VLOOKUP).
- **Combine** by **Position**: pair the first item of input 1 with the first item of input 2, and so on. Only safe when both lists are in the same order.
- **Combine** with **All Possible Combinations**: every item of one input with every item of the other.
- **SQL Query**: write a **query** (a question about data) in **SQL**, a language for asking questions of tables, using `input1`, `input2`.
- **Choose Branch**: output the data of one input only, used to wait for both branches to finish.

Example: a Schedule trigger fetches today's orders from Shopify and all customers from a Google Sheet in two branches. A Merge node in Matching Fields mode joins them on `email`, so each order item now carries the customer's tier.

Gotchas:

- The order of the inputs matters for some options; check which branch goes into input 1.
- If one input receives no items, the result may be empty. Test with realistic data on both sides.
- Field names must match exactly, including capitalisation, or nothing pairs up.
takeaways: Append stacks items; Combine joins them
Matching Fields is a lookup between two data sources
Check input order and field names when results are empty
pitfalls: Using Combine by Position on lists that are not in the same order, which pairs the wrong records.

quiz.q: You want each order to get the matching customer's tier from another source, joined on email. Which mode?
quiz.explain: Matching Fields pairs items whose email values match.

concepts.name: Loops and batching
concepts.summary: Know when n8n loops for you, when to use Loop Over Items in batches, and how to slow down for rate limits.
concepts.why: Calling an app with hundreds of items at once can hit limits; batching keeps workflows reliable.
concepts.body:
A **loop** means doing the same steps again for each thing in a list. In n8n you usually don't need to build one: most nodes already run once per item, as you learned.

You do need an explicit loop when:

- An app limits how many requests you may send per minute (a **rate limit**), so you must slow down.
- You want to handle items in groups (**batches**) with the same steps, one group at a time.
- A node only handles the first item, or only runs once. Some database actions, and some nodes covered later (custom code, sub-workflows) in their "run once for all items" mode, work this way.

The **Loop Over Items** node (formerly called Split in Batches) does this. Set a **Batch Size** (how many items per group): with 1, items are handled one at a time; with 50, fifty at a time. Connect the steps you want to repeat to its **loop** output, and connect the last of those steps back into the Loop Over Items node. When all items are processed, the **done** output continues the workflow. It stops by itself, so you don't need an If node to end it.

To respect rate limits, add a **Wait** node inside the loop, for example 2 seconds per batch.

For "keep going until a condition is true" loops (such as fetching pages from an API until there are no more), connect a later node back to an earlier one and use an If node to decide when to stop. The HTTP Request node (which calls any API, covered soon) can also fetch page after page by itself, called **pagination**.
takeaways: Most nodes already run per item; explicit loops are for batching and special cases
Loop Over Items: steps on the loop output, connect back, continue from done
Add a Wait node inside the loop to respect rate limits
pitfalls: Forgetting to connect the last node in the loop back to Loop Over Items, so only the first batch runs.

quiz.q: An API allows only 60 requests per minute and you have 500 items. What's a good approach?
options: Loop Over Items with a small batch size and a Wait node
quiz.explain: Batching plus a pause keeps the request rate under the API's limit.

concepts.name: Expressions in depth: nodes, dates, variables
concepts.summary: Reach any earlier node by name, work with dates using $now, use helpers like $if, and read workflow variables.
concepts.why: Real workflows need data from several steps back, dates and fallbacks, not just the previous node's fields.
concepts.body:
`$json` only reaches the data of the node directly before. Often you need something from further back, such as the original trigger.

**Referencing other nodes.** `$('Node name')` reaches any earlier node by its name:

- `{{ $('Get customer').item.json.plan }}`: the plan from the "Get customer" node, for the item that matches the current one. n8n tracks which output item came from which input item (called **item linking** or paired items), so `.item` follows that link.
- `.first()` and `.all()` give the first item or all items of that node.

This is why clear node names matter: renaming a node updates expressions, but names like `HTTP Request3` make them unreadable.

**Dates.** `$now` is the current date and time, and `$today` is midnight today, both in the workflow's time zone (the region's clock chosen in its settings). They come with formatting helpers from Luxon, a ready-made date toolkit (a **library** of code others can reuse): `{{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}` or `{{ $now.plus({ days: 7 }).toISODate() }}`.

**Helpers.**

- `$if(condition, valueIfTrue, valueIfFalse)`: a quick either/or.
- `$ifEmpty(value, fallback)`: use a fallback when a field is empty.
- `$jmespath()`: pick values out of deeply nested JSON using a short search pattern.

**Context.** `$execution` (the current run, including its ID), `$workflow` (name, ID) and `$vars` (shared **variables**, settings stored once and reused across workflows, on plans that include them).

If an expression grows past one line, a data node or the Code node (where you write a small program, covered later) is usually clearer.
takeaways: $('Node name').item.json.field reaches earlier nodes via item linking
$now and $today with Luxon helpers handle dates
$if, $ifEmpty and $vars cover common needs

quiz.q: Three nodes after the trigger, you need the trigger's email field. What should you use?
quiz.explain: $json only sees the previous node; $('Node name') reaches any earlier node.

concepts.name: HTTP Request: call any API
concepts.summary: Use the HTTP Request node to talk to services that have no ready-made n8n node, setting each part of the request from the API docs.
concepts.why: With HTTP Request, n8n can work with almost any web service, not just the built-in integrations.
concepts.body:
Hundreds of apps have their own n8n node, but many services don't. As long as a service has an **API** (a documented way for programs to send it requests and get answers), the **HTTP Request** node can use it. It is named after **HTTP**, the set of rules the web uses to send requests and responses.

A request has a few parts, all described in the service's API documentation:

- **HTTP method**: what you want to do. **GET** reads data, **POST** creates something, PATCH or PUT updates, DELETE removes.
- **URL**: the address of the thing you want, such as `https://api.example.com/v1/customers`.
- **Authentication** (proving who you are): prefer **Predefined Credential Type** when n8n already knows the service, so you reuse a normal credential. Otherwise use a general-purpose type such as Header Auth (an API key sent in a header, an extra labelled line of the request) or OAuth2.
- **Query parameters**: options added to the end of the URL after a `?`, such as `?status=open`.
- **Headers**: extra labelled information.
- **Body**: the data you send with POST or PUT, usually JSON.

Shortcut: API docs often show examples as a **cURL** command: a line of text you would type to run cURL, a small tool programmers use to send web requests. Click `Import cURL`, paste it, and n8n fills in the node.

The response becomes items for the next node. Useful options: **Pagination** fetches page after page of results automatically, for services that return long lists a page at a time; "Never Error" lets you handle failed responses yourself; batching sends requests in small groups (**batches**) with pauses between them.

The same node can also be given to an AI agent (covered in the AI chapter) as a tool, with options to trim long responses so they use fewer tokens.

Never paste API keys into the URL or body; keep them in credentials.
takeaways: HTTP Request reaches any service with an API
HTTP method, URL, authentication, query parameters, headers and body come from the API docs
Paste cURL examples to fill the node, use built-in pagination; keep keys in credentials
pitfalls: Putting an API key directly in the URL, where it ends up saved in the Executions list for anyone with access to see.

quiz.q: The API docs say "POST /v1/tickets with a JSON body". What does POST indicate?
quiz.explain: POST is the method normally used to create a new resource.

concepts.name: Webhooks: start workflows from any system
concepts.summary: Use the Webhook node to receive data from other systems, understand test vs live (production) URLs, and send a response back.
concepts.why: Webhooks let other apps start your workflow instantly and even turn a workflow into a small API.
concepts.body:
A **webhook** is an automatic message one system sends to a web address when something happens: "invoice paid", "form submitted". The **Webhook** trigger node gives your workflow such an address.

Each Webhook node has two URLs:

- The **test URL** works only while you click "Listen for test event" in the editor. The incoming data appears in the node so you can build the next steps.
- The **production URL** works once the workflow is published. Its runs show up in the Executions list, not on the canvas.

Give the production URL to the sending system. Mixing the two up is the most common webhook problem.

Settings:

- **HTTP method**: the kind of request the sender makes, usually POST (sends data in the body) or GET (asks for data).
- **Authentication**: a check that the caller is allowed, such as Basic Auth (a username and password) or Header Auth (a secret key sent along with each call), so strangers can't trigger your workflow. You can also accept calls only from a list of approved computer addresses.
- **Respond**: "Immediately" (reply right away, then keep working), "When Last Node Finishes" (reply with the final result), or "Using 'Respond to Webhook' Node" (you decide exactly what to send back and when). AI chat workflows can also send their reply bit by bit as it is written.

With "When Last Node Finishes" or Respond to Webhook, your workflow becomes a small API: another app sends a question and gets n8n's computed answer.

The incoming data (`body`), the extra labels sent with it (`headers`) and any options in the URL (`query`) all appear in the item, so the email in the example below would be reached with `{{ $json.body.customer.email }}`. By default one incoming message can be at most 16 MB (**megabytes**; a phone photo is typically 2 to 5 MB).
takeaways: Test URL for building, production URL after publishing
Protect webhooks with authentication
Choose how to respond: immediately, at the end, or via Respond to Webhook
pitfalls: Configuring the sending app with the test URL, which stops working as soon as you stop listening.

quiz.q: Your webhook works while you click "Listen for test event" but not in daily use. What is the likely cause?
options: The sender uses the test URL, or the workflow isn't published
quiz.explain: Live traffic needs the production URL of a published workflow.

concepts.name: The AI Agent node: model, prompt and chat
concepts.summary: Build your first AI agent with the AI Agent node, a chat model sub-node and a Chat Trigger, and control it with a system message.
concepts.why: The AI Agent node is the center of n8n's AI features; everything else plugs into it.
concepts.body:
n8n's AI features are built on **LangChain**, a popular free toolkit for building apps on large language models (LLMs).

In the editor they appear as **cluster nodes**: one main **root node** with smaller **sub-nodes** plugged into its bottom connectors.

The most important root node is the **AI Agent**. An AI agent is an AI that works towards a goal on its own: unlike a fixed chain of steps, it lets the model decide what to do next, including which **tools** (actions it can call, next lesson) to use. Its sub-node slots are:

- **Chat Model** (required): which model to use, from providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or models running on your own computer through Ollama. You need a credential for the provider (on Cloud, n8n's built-in AI credits may cover it). Model names change often, so pick from the current list.
- **Chat memory**: lets the agent remember earlier messages in a conversation.
- **Tools**: what it can do beyond writing text.
- An optional **output parser**, which makes the answer come back in a fixed shape, such as named fields.

The quickest start: add a **Chat Trigger** ("When chat message received"), connect an AI Agent, plug in a chat model, and click Open chat. Each message you type becomes the agent's prompt.

The agent can also be fed by any other node, for example an email body, using an expression for the prompt.

In the node's options, the **System Message** (n8n's name for the system prompt) sets standing instructions: role, tone, rules, what to do when unsure. Another option limits how many steps it may take.

For simple one-shot jobs (summarise, sort into categories), the **Basic LLM Chain** node or the **Text Classifier** node (sorts text into categories you set) is cheaper and more predictable than an agent.
takeaways: AI nodes are cluster nodes: a root node plus sub-nodes
AI Agent needs a chat model; chat memory and tools are added as sub-nodes
Use the System Message for standing instructions; use chains for simple one-shot tasks

quiz.q: Which sub-node must every AI Agent have to work?
quiz.explain: The chat model is the LLM that does the thinking; the others are optional add-ons.

concepts.name: Error handling: retries and error workflows
concepts.summary: Make workflows survive failures with Retry On Fail, error outputs, the Stop and Error node, and a central error workflow.
concepts.why: Published workflows run unattended; without a plan for errors, failures go unnoticed until someone complains.
concepts.body:
Sooner or later a node fails: an API is down, a record is missing, data is badly formed. n8n gives you tools at three levels.

**Per node** (in the node's Settings tab):

- **Retry On Fail**: try again a few times with a pause (a **retry**). Good for brief outages, when a service is down for a minute.
- **On Error**: by default the workflow stops. You can instead choose to continue, or to continue using an **error output**: the node gets an extra output, and failed items go down that branch, where you might write them to a sheet or notify someone while good items carry on.

**Deliberate failures.** The **Stop and Error** node fails the run on purpose with your own message, for example when a required field is missing. That's better than letting bad data continue.

**Per workflow: error workflows.** Build a separate workflow that starts with the **Error Trigger** node and sends an alert (Slack, email, a ticket). Then, in each important workflow's Settings, choose it as the **Error workflow**. Whenever a production run fails, the error workflow receives details: workflow name and ID, the execution ID and URL, the last node that ran, and the error message. One error workflow can serve all your workflows.

**Afterwards**, open the failed execution in the Executions list, fix the cause, and retry it.

Design tip: make workflows safe to run twice (check whether a record exists before creating it), because retries and re-runs will happen.
takeaways: Retry On Fail handles brief outages
Error outputs let failed items take their own branch
A central error workflow (Error Trigger) alerts you about failed runs
pitfalls: Setting nodes to "continue" on error without recording the failures anywhere, so they disappear silently.

quiz.q: Which node must an error workflow start with?
quiz.explain: The Error Trigger receives the details of the failed execution.

concepts.name: Sub-workflows: reusable building blocks
concepts.summary: Split big workflows into smaller ones and call them with Execute Sub-workflow, passing defined inputs and getting results back.
concepts.why: Sub-workflows keep large automations readable and let several workflows share one tested piece of logic.
concepts.body:
Big workflows with 60 nodes become hard to read and test. **Sub-workflows** let you split them, like moving a repeated recipe step into its own card.

A sub-workflow is a normal workflow that starts with the **Execute Workflow Trigger** (shown as "When Executed by Another Workflow"). It defines what input it accepts:

- **Define using fields below**: name each input and its type, such as `email` (text, which n8n calls a **string**) and `amount` (number). Callers then see exactly these fields.
- **Define using JSON example**: paste a sample of the expected data.
- **Accept all data**: anything goes, so the sub-workflow must cope with missing values.

In the parent workflow, the **Execute Sub-workflow** node picks the sub-workflow and maps data into its inputs. The data produced by the sub-workflow's last node comes back as the node's output. You can also choose to not wait for the result, for fire-and-forget jobs (start it and move on).

Uses:

- Shared logic: "find or create customer" used by ten workflows.
- Smaller pieces that are easier to test in isolation.
- Tools for AI agents: the **Call n8n Workflow Tool** lets an agent run a sub-workflow (next lessons).
- Lighter load: the data a sub-workflow handles is cleared from the computer's working memory when it finishes, which helps with big jobs.

In the editor you can select nodes and convert them into a sub-workflow directly.

Note for n8n 2.x: when a sub-workflow pauses (waiting for a webhook, form or approval) and resumes, the parent now receives the sub-workflow's final output.
takeaways: Sub-workflows start with the Execute Workflow Trigger
Define inputs explicitly so callers know what to send
Execute Sub-workflow passes data in and returns the last node's output

quiz.q: Which input mode makes the sub-workflow's expected fields clear to every caller?
quiz.explain: Named, typed fields appear in the calling node, so callers know exactly what to map.

concepts.name: The Code node (JavaScript and Python)
concepts.summary: Write small JavaScript or Python snippets in the Code node when built-in nodes get awkward, and know its limits in n8n 2.x.
concepts.why: A few lines of code can replace a tangle of nodes, but only if you know how items go in and out.
concepts.body:
Sometimes the visual nodes get clumsy, such as complex calculations or picking apart unusual text. The **Code** node runs a short program you write. It supports **JavaScript** and **Python** (two popular programming languages). If you don't code, AI assistants can draft snippets, but have someone who codes review them before you rely on them.

Two modes decide how often your code runs:

- **Run Once for All Items** (default): your code gets every item at once (`$input.all()` in JavaScript) and returns a list of items.
- **Run Once for Each Item**: your code runs per item and works on `$json`, the current item.

Whatever you return must be items: a list in which each item keeps its fields inside a `json` part. n8n adds the `json` wrapper if you forget it, but returning the right shape avoids surprises.

Python in n8n 2.x runs through **task runners**: separate helper programs that run your code apart from n8n itself, so a mistake in your code can't harm n8n. It uses `_items` and `_item` instead of `$input`, and needs square brackets to reach fields, like `item["json"]["price"]`. The older Python option (called Pyodide) was removed in 2.0, so old Python snippets may need updating.

Limits:

- The Code node can't call websites or read files directly; use the HTTP Request node and file nodes.
- In 2.x it can't read the settings stored on the server (its **environment variables**) by default.
- On Cloud, extra libraries aren't available (JavaScript has `crypto` and `moment`); self-hosters can allow more.
- Never put secrets in code; use credentials (n8n's saved logins).

If the logic fits in Edit Fields or an expression, prefer that: others can read it without coding.
takeaways: Choose Run Once for All Items or Run Once for Each Item
Return a list of items with fields under json
In 2.x, Python runs in separate task runners; no direct web calls, files or environment variables
pitfalls: Copying a 1.x Pyodide Python snippet that reaches fields with dots; the new Python needs item["json"]["field"].

quiz.q: In "Run Once for All Items" mode, what should your code return?
options: A list of items, each with a json object
quiz.explain: The Code node outputs items, so it must return a list of objects with their fields under json.

concepts.name: Agent tools, memory and human review
concepts.summary: Give an agent tools (app nodes, web requests, sub-workflows), let the model fill parameters with $fromAI, add chat memory, and require approval for risky calls.
concepts.why: Tools turn an agent from a chatbot into something that does work, and approvals keep that work safe.
concepts.body:
A **tool** is an action the agent may decide to call: look up an order, create a ticket, send a message. The model reads each tool's name and description, chooses one, fills in its inputs, reads the result, and repeats until it can answer.

Kinds of tools you can plug into the Tools slot:

- **App nodes as tools**: many app nodes (Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack...) have a tool version.
- **HTTP Request Tool**: any API.
- **Call n8n Workflow Tool**: runs one of your sub-workflows, the best way to give an agent a carefully controlled multi-step action.
- **MCP Client Tool**: uses tools that another system offers through **MCP** (Model Context Protocol), a standard way for AI apps to share tools. A system offering tools this way is called an MCP server.

**Who fills the inputs?** Fix everything you can (for example the spreadsheet ID). For values only the model can know, click the sparkle button on the field, or write `{{ $fromAI('email', 'customer email address') }}`. The key and description are hints the model uses to choose a value.

Write clear tool names and descriptions; the model picks tools based on them.

**Chat memory.** Without it each message is a fresh start. **Simple Memory** keeps the last few messages of a conversation; Postgres Chat Memory or Redis Chat Memory store the history in a database (Postgres and Redis are two popular ones) so it survives restarts. Keep the window small: everything remembered is sent to the model each time.

**Human review.** Having a person approve a step before it takes effect is called human review. In the agent's tools panel you can add a **Human review** step and connect risky tools to it. Before such a tool runs, the workflow pauses and asks a person (in n8n Chat, Slack, Teams, Gmail and others) to approve or deny. Denied calls are cancelled and the agent is told so.
takeaways: Tools: app nodes, HTTP Request, sub-workflows and MCP servers
Fix what you can; use $fromAI only for values the model must choose
Add chat memory for conversations and Human review for risky tools
pitfalls: Giving an agent a delete or send tool with every field left to the model and no human review.

quiz.q: What does {{ $fromAI('email', 'customer email') }} do in a tool parameter?
options: Reads the email from the previous node
Lets the model supply the value when it calls the tool
quiz.explain: $fromAI marks a parameter the model fills in, using the key and description as hints.

concepts.name: Vector stores and RAG
concepts.summary: Let an agent answer from your own documents: load and split them, store them in a vector store, and attach the store as a tool.
concepts.why: Models only know what they learned in training; RAG makes them answer from your current documents.
concepts.body:
Ask a model about your refund policy and it will guess, because your policy wasn't in the text it learned from (its **training data**). **RAG** (retrieval-augmented generation) fixes this: before answering, the system looks up the relevant passages in your documents and gives them to the model.

The lookup uses **embeddings**: lists of numbers that capture what a piece of text means, so texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. A **vector store** is a database that stores these numbers and finds the closest matches to a question, even when the wording differs.

**Step 1: insert your documents** (a separate workflow you run when documents change):

- Fetch the files (Google Drive, a website, a database).
- A vector store node in **Insert Documents** mode: for example **Simple Vector Store** for testing, or a specialised database such as Pinecone, Qdrant, Supabase or Postgres PGVector for real use.
- Plug in an **Embeddings** sub-node (the model that turns text into numbers).
- Plug in a **Default Data Loader** with a **text splitter** that cuts documents into chunks (small passages); this cutting is called **chunking**. The Recursive Character Text Splitter is a good default. Add **metadata** (labels about each chunk, such as its source or date).

**Step 2: search.** Attach the same vector store to your AI Agent as a tool, with a description such as "Search the company handbook". Set how many chunks to return. You must use the **same embeddings model** as for insertion, otherwise searches return nonsense.

Keep chunks focused, return a handful rather than dozens (they all cost tokens), and tell the agent in its system message to say "I don't know" when the search finds nothing relevant.

Simple Vector Store keeps everything in the computer's working memory, so it is lost whenever n8n restarts: use a real database in production.
takeaways: RAG = retrieve relevant chunks, then let the model answer from them
Insert: loader + splitter + embeddings into a vector store
Search with the same embeddings model; attach the store as an agent tool
pitfalls: Inserting with one embeddings model and searching with another, which makes search results meaningless.

quiz.q: Why does the query side need the same embeddings model as the insert side?
options: Different models produce incompatible numbers, so similarity search breaks
Vector stores require one model per account
quiz.explain: Similarity only makes sense between vectors produced by the same embeddings model.

concepts.name: Self-hosting n8n with Docker
concepts.summary: Run n8n yourself with Docker: keep its data and encryption key safe, use a proper database, set the time zone, update, and serve it securely.
concepts.why: Self-hosting gives you control over data and cost, but you become responsible for keeping n8n safe and running.
concepts.body:
Self-hosting means running n8n on a computer you control, usually a cloud server. The recommended way is **Docker**: a tool that runs software in a **container**, a sealed box holding the program and everything it needs, so it runs the same on any computer.

**Docker Compose** describes several containers (n8n, a database) in one settings file, so they start together.

Key pieces:

- **Image**: the ready-to-run download of n8n, called `n8nio/n8n`. Fix it to an exact version number (for example `2.43.8`) rather than "latest", so updates happen only when you choose. This is called **version pinning**. In 2.x the release channels are called `stable` and `beta`.
- **Volume**: a storage folder that survives container restarts. Attach one at the folder `/home/node/.n8n`. It holds the **encryption key** that protects all credentials. Lose it, and saved credentials can't be decrypted.
- **Database**: n8n uses SQLite (a single-file database) by default. For production use **PostgreSQL**, a sturdier database, via `DB_TYPE=postgresdb` and the `DB_POSTGRESDB_*` settings. MySQL is no longer supported for n8n's own data in 2.x.
- **Settings** are **environment variables** (named values handed to the container when it starts), such as `GENERIC_TIMEZONE` and `TZ` for schedules, and `WEBHOOK_URL` so webhook URLs show your public address.
- **HTTPS** (the secure, padlocked kind of web address): put n8n behind a **reverse proxy**, a front server such as Caddy, Traefik or nginx that receives all visitors first. It holds the security **certificate** (a digital ID card that proves the site is really yours), so logins and webhooks are encrypted.

Updating: pull the new image, then recreate the container. Read the release notes first, back up the database and the `.n8n` folder, and test on a copy for major versions.

You are now the one in charge: **backups** (saved copies you can restore from), updates, checking that it stays up, and security are your job.
concepts.code:
docker volume create n8n_data
docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 \
  -e GENERIC_TIMEZONE="Europe/Berlin" -e TZ="Europe/Berlin" \
  -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n \
  n8nio/n8n
# then open http://localhost:5678
takeaways: Run n8n with Docker (Compose for production) and a .n8n volume that keeps its data
Back up the encryption key and the database
Use PostgreSQL, pin versions, and serve over HTTPS
pitfalls: Running without a volume, so every restart wipes workflows and the encryption key.

quiz.q: Why is the /home/node/.n8n volume so important?
options: It holds the n8n program itself
It keeps data, including the encryption key for credentials, across restarts
quiz.explain: Without it, restarts lose data and the key needed to decrypt saved credentials.

concepts.name: Scaling with queue mode
concepts.summary: Handle heavy load on self-hosted n8n with queue mode: a main instance hands runs to separate workers through a shared waiting line.
concepts.why: One running copy of n8n can't keep up with heavy load; queue mode spreads executions across many workers.
concepts.body:
By default one running copy of n8n (one **process**, as computers call a running program) does everything: shows the editor, receives webhooks, and runs every execution. Under heavy load (many webhooks, long AI runs) it becomes the **bottleneck**: the slow point that holds everything up. **Queue mode** splits the work.

The parts:

- **Main instance**: the main copy of n8n (each running n8n installation is an **instance**). It serves the editor and API, handles schedules and incoming webhooks, and creates executions. It does not run them; it puts their IDs in a **queue** (a waiting line, first in, first out).
- **Redis**: a very fast database, used here as the **message broker**: the waiting line where executions sit until a worker picks them up.
- **Workers**: separate n8n processes whose only job is running executions. They are started with `n8n worker`. Each takes executions from Redis, loads the workflow from the database, runs it and saves the result. Add more workers to handle more load.
- **PostgreSQL**: one shared database for all of them. SQLite isn't supported here.
- Optional **webhook processors** (`n8n webhook`) behind a **load balancer** (a server that spreads incoming requests across several copies) for very high webhook traffic.

Configuration essentials:

- Set `EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue` and the Redis connection settings on every process.
- Every worker and webhook processor must use the **same** `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` as the main instance, or they can't unlock the saved credentials.
- Worker **concurrency** (how many executions one worker runs at the same time) defaults to 10; n8n advises at least 5, since many workers each doing little can swamp the database with connections.
- Files that workflows handle can't be kept on just one machine, because a different worker may need them; use S3-compatible storage (an online file store like Amazon S3).

Enterprise self-hosted plans add **multi-main** setups (several main instances) for **high availability**: n8n keeps working even if one of them fails.

Measure first: deleting old execution data and lighter workflows often fix slowness before scaling is needed.
takeaways: Main instance queues executions in Redis; workers run them
All processes share PostgreSQL and the same encryption key
Use S3 storage for files and tune worker concurrency
pitfalls: Starting workers with a different N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, so every credential fails to decrypt on them.

quiz.q: In queue mode, which component actually runs the workflow executions?
quiz.explain: The main instance queues execution IDs in Redis; workers pick them up and run them.

concepts.name: Versions, source control and environments
concepts.summary: Move workflows safely from a test copy of n8n to the live one, using Git to carry them across without their secrets.
concepts.why: Editing production directly is risky; environments let teams test changes before they go live.
concepts.body:
Inside one **instance** (one installed copy of n8n), **version history** already lets you restore and compare versions: n8n can show a visual **diff**, a side-by-side view of what changed between two versions. For teams this isn't enough: you want to try changes on a **development** instance and promote them to **production** only when tested. Each separate n8n instance is called an **environment**.

n8n connects instances through **Git**, the standard system for tracking changes to files. Tracking changes like this is called **version control** (n8n calls the feature source control). A Git **repository** (a shared, versioned folder, often on GitHub or GitLab) sits between the instances. Typically each environment is linked to its own **branch** (a separate line of changes in the repository).

What gets pushed to Git:

- Workflows you choose, with their tags.
- **Credential stubs**: only the name, type and ID, never the secret values. You create the real credentials separately on each instance, under the same names.
- **Variable stubs** (names of shared settings, without values), tags, folders, projects, and the layout of n8n's data tables (but not the data in them).

Recommended flow is one direction: build on dev, push to Git, pull on production. Don't push and pull on the same instance. n8n can't detect conflicting edits to a workflow, so a pull can overwrite local changes.

Pushing sends the **saved** version, not the published one. After pulling on production, publish the workflows there.

Permissions: instance owners, admins and project admins can push; owners and admins can pull. Source control is a feature of the paid self-hosted and enterprise plans. You can also automate promotion through n8n's API.
takeaways: Environments are separate instances linked through a Git repository
Credentials travel only as credential stubs; secrets are created per instance
Promote one way (dev to Git to prod), then publish on production
pitfalls: Pushing and pulling on the same instance and overwriting someone's unpushed changes.

quiz.q: When you push credentials to Git, what is included?
options: Only stubs: name, type and ID
quiz.explain: n8n pushes credential stubs; actual secrets are created separately on each instance.

concepts.name: Security hardening for n8n
concepts.summary: Lock down n8n: company logins and two-step sign-in, blocked nodes, isolated code, limits on what it may call, hidden data, audits and safe agents.
concepts.why: n8n holds credentials to many systems; a hacked n8n or a misled agent can do real damage.
concepts.body:
An n8n **instance** (one installed copy of n8n) holds keys to many of your systems. Treat it like a sensitive server.

**Access**

- Use **SSO** (single sign-on: staff log in with their existing company account) where available.
- Require **two-factor authentication** (2FA): proving who you are with two things, your password and a code from your phone.
- Give people the lowest role they need, and use projects to limit who sees which credentials.

**Instance settings** (self-hosted)

- Serve only over HTTPS, and keep the encryption key secret; replace (rotate) it if it is ever exposed.
- **Block nodes** you don't need. n8n 2.x already disables Execute Command and Local File Trigger (nodes that run commands on the server or watch its files) by default, restricts file nodes to one folder, and blocks environment-variable access from the Code node.
- **Harden task runners**, the helper programs that run the code from Code nodes apart from n8n itself.
- Enable **SSRF protection**. SSRF (server-side request forgery) means tricking a server into calling addresses it shouldn't. The protection limits which addresses nodes may call, so a workflow can't be used to poke around your company's internal systems.
- Disable the public API if unused, and consider **execution data redaction** so sensitive inputs don't stay visible in the Executions list.
- Run the built-in **security audit**, which reports risky settings, nodes and credentials.

**Workflows**: protect webhooks with authentication, and check incoming data before using it (**validation**) with If or Stop and Error nodes.

**AI agents**: text an agent reads (an email, a web page, a document) may contain instructions written to manipulate it, called **prompt injection**. Give agents only the tools they need, fix parameters instead of using `$fromAI` where possible, and put Human review on tools that send, change or delete.
takeaways: SSO, 2FA and the lowest roles people need protect access
Block unneeded nodes, harden task runners, enable SSRF protection, run audits
Treat agent inputs as untrusted: few tools, fixed parameters, human review
pitfalls: Re-enabling Execute Command on a shared instance, which lets any editor run commands on the server.

quiz.q: An agent reads customer emails and has a "delete record" tool. What reduces the risk most?
options: Human review on the delete tool and limiting which records it can touch
quiz.explain: Emails can contain manipulative instructions; approvals and narrow permissions limit the damage.

concepts.name: MCP: n8n as server and client
concepts.summary: Let AI assistants use your n8n workflows through MCP, for your whole n8n or for one workflow, and let n8n agents use outside MCP tools.
concepts.why: MCP connects n8n to the wider AI ecosystem in both directions, with real security implications.
concepts.body:
**MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI assistants discover and call tools provided by other systems. An **MCP server** offers tools; an **MCP client** (the app that uses them, such as Claude Desktop, Cursor or an n8n agent) calls them. n8n can play both roles.

**n8n as a server: instance-level MCP.** An owner or admin turns on **Enable MCP access** in Settings. Assistants then connect to one URL for your whole n8n installation (ending in `/mcp-server/http`), signing in with OAuth or an API key. Nothing is exposed by default: you mark each workflow (or a whole project or folder) as available in MCP. Connected assistants can search workflows, run the exposed ones, and in recent 2.x versions also create and edit workflows and data tables. Access follows the signed-in user's permissions.

**n8n as a server: MCP Server Trigger.** This node turns a single workflow into its own MCP server with specific tools attached. Use it for a small, self-contained tool set; use instance-level access for broad use.

**n8n as a client.** Give an AI Agent the **MCP Client Tool** to use tools from an external MCP server. Recent versions also offer some popular MCP servers directly in the agent's tools panel.

Design advice:

- Expose workflows with clear names, descriptions and defined inputs (sub-workflow style), not your whole instance.
- Treat every MCP call like a webhook from the outside: check its inputs before using them.
- Assistants act on whatever they read, so keep write actions behind Human review.
- Revoke API keys and OAuth grants you no longer use.
takeaways: Instance-level MCP exposes chosen workflows to assistants through one URL
MCP Server Trigger makes one workflow an MCP server; MCP Client Tool consumes others
Expose little, check inputs, and keep approvals on write actions

quiz.q: After enabling instance-level MCP, which workflows can an assistant run?
options: None until you publish to Git
Only workflows you explicitly made available in MCP
quiz.explain: Nothing is exposed by default; you enable each workflow, folder or project.
